name: Dynamic dispatch
summary: The function a call runs is chosen at run time from the object it’s called on, usually through a table of function pointers.
howItWorks: With dynamic dispatch the code making a call doesn’t know which function will run; the object it’s called on decides. In C++ and Rust the usual mechanism is a vtable: a table of function pointers for each type, and every object (C++) or reference (Rust) carries a pointer to its type’s table. A call loads the right entry and jumps through it, which costs one extra memory load and an indirect call. C++ does this for `virtual` methods, Rust for `dyn Trait`, Go for interface values, C# for `virtual` and interface methods, and Java for most methods. Python and JavaScript look methods up by name on the object, so any object with the right method will do, which Python calls duck typing. The bigger cost is what the compiler loses: it can’t see which function runs, so it can’t inline it and optimize across the call. JIT compilers win much of that back. The HotSpot JVM inlines virtual calls that in practice reach one class and undoes it if a new class loads; V8 caches the lookup at each call site. In return, one compiled copy of the code serves every type, one list can mix types, and new types can arrive after compiling: plugins, user subclasses, test fakes.
analogy: Calling a company’s front desk instead of someone’s direct line. You dial the same number whoever is on shift and get put through; it takes a moment longer, but staff can come and go without reprinting anyone’s phone book.
useWhen: One collection holds different types behind a shared interface: shapes on a canvas, middleware in a chain, UI widgets
Plugins, drivers or library users add implementations after your code is compiled
Swapping an implementation at run time or in tests, such as a fake payment gateway
Keeping build time and binary size down when a generic would be compiled for many types
avoidWhen: Tight loops where a tiny method is called per element, such as per pixel; prefer static dispatch or move the loop inside the method
Every type is known at compile time and speed matters; generics let the compiler inline
example: A drawing app keeps its shapes in a `Vec<Box<dyn Shape>>`: circles, squares and shapes added by plugins, all in one list. Redrawing loops over the list and calls `area()` on each, loading the function from that shape’s vtable. The loop is compiled once, works for shape types that didn’t exist when it was compiled, and pays an indirect call per shape that the compiler can’t inline.

source: // A &dyn Shape is two pointers: the data and the type's vtable
shapes.iter().map(|s| s.area()).sum()  // area() is looked up in each vtable
Box::new(Square { s: 2.0 }),          // different types, one Vec
println!("{}", total_area(&shapes));   // total_area is compiled once

story: Bjarne Stroustrup borrowed virtual functions from Simula and added them to C++ in 1983, and he called them the feature with the greatest impact on how C++ was written. His implementation was deliberately simple: the virtual functions of a class form an array of function pointers, each object holds one pointer to its class’s array, and a virtual call is an indirect call through it. Colleagues were skeptical; some argued virtual functions were a crippled function pointer and a needless inefficiency. He added them anyway.

Dynamic languages had it worse. In Smalltalk-80 every operation is a message send, so finding the method for each send was both expensive and critical. In 1984 Peter Deutsch and Allan Schiffman noticed that at a given call site the receiver is usually the same class as last time, so they cached the looked-up method right at the call site and only re-checked the class: the inline cache. In 1991 Urs Hölzle, Craig Chambers and David Ungar extended it for the Self language to hold several classes per call site, and used the classes it recorded to recompile hot code with calls inlined.

Today’s virtual machines rely on the same ideas. The HotSpot JVM profiles running code, inlines virtual calls and deoptimizes when a newly loaded class invalidates its assumptions, and V8 gives every JavaScript object a hidden class so its inline caches can work. Newer languages make the cost visible instead: Rust 1.27 (2018) added the `dyn Trait` syntax because the old trait-object syntax looked like an ordinary type and hid that calls were dispatched at run time.

choices.choice: One table per class, one pointer per object
choices.why: Stroustrup wanted a virtual call to be about as efficient in time and space as an ordinary function call as typically used. A per-class array and a single indirect call kept it cheap and predictable.

choices.choice: Cache the lookup at the call site
choices.why: Smalltalk systems already used a global method cache keyed by class and selector. Deutsch and Schiffman saw that most call sites see the same class every time, so a one-entry cache in the code itself skips the lookup on most calls.

choices.choice: Several cached classes per call site
choices.why: Some call sites really are polymorphic. Polymorphic inline caches kept a short list of classes and, as a side effect, recorded which types actually occur, so the compiler could inline the common cases later. Self programs ran a median 11% faster from the caches alone, and 27% faster with that recompilation.
Rust’s designers came to regret that `Box<Foo>` could mean a trait object. Writing `Box<dyn Foo>` makes it obvious where calls go through a vtable and cost an indirect call.
